title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 12: old Pelagian cantilena — Prosper, Faustus, Augustine's defense loci
pass_a_gloss: Solution. It was an ancient ditty of the Pelagians, that those induce fate and destroy free choice who establish an absolute and efficacious predestination of certain human beings before foresight of merits. That may be seen in Prosper, who writes that the Pelagians defamed Augustine, saying that He utterly removes free choice, and under the name of grace preaches a fatal necessity, On free choice p. 223. The same objection occurs also in his Responses to the chapters of the Gauls Obj. 6. Further Faustus of Riez, coryphaeus of the Semipelagians, obliquely wounds Augustine, and calls him the destroyer of free choice, who pronounces all things on either side to be established and defined from predestination, On free choice book 1 section 11. And he says that under the word of grace a fatal decree is hidden by him, in the same place. Finally, Augustine himself in many places is compelled to wash away this most unfair calumny: Against the two Epistles of the Pelagians book 2 chapter 7, and On the Good of Perseverance book 2 chapter 12, and elsewhere everywhere. These things I wished to premise to our answer, that you may understand from whose pools nearly all the adversaries' arguments are drawn.
pass_b_english: Sol. An old Pelagian refrain: those who hold absolute, efficacious predestination of certain people before foresight of merits induce fate and destroy free choice. Prosper records Pelagians defaming Augustine as utterly removing free choice and preaching fatal necessity under the name of grace (De lib. arb. p. 223). The same charge is in his Responses to the Gallic chapters, Obj. 6. Faustus of Riez, Semipelagian champion, obliquely strikes Augustine as destroyer of free choice for saying everything on either side is fixed by predestination (De lib. arb. 1.11), and claims a fatal decree is hidden under the word grace. Augustine himself must often wash off that foul calumny (Contra 2 Epist. Pelag. 2.7; De bono persever. 2.12; and elsewhere). I premise this so you see from whose cisterns almost all the adversaries' arguments are drawn.
source_text: Sol. Antiqua fuit Pelagianorum cantilena, eos fatum inducere et liberum arbitrium perimere, qui statuunt absolutam et efficacem certorum hominum praedestinationem ante praescientiam meritorum. Id videre licet apud Prosperum, qui scribit Pelagianos infamasse Augustinum, dicentes Eum liberum arbitrium penitus submovere, et sub gratiae nomine necessitatem praedicare fatalem, De lib. arbit. pag. 223. Eadem objectio occurrit etiam in Responsionibus ejusdem ad capitula Gallorum Obj. 6. Porro Faustus Regiensis Semipelagianorum coryphaeus oblique perstringit Augustinum, et appellat liberi arbitrii interemtorem, qui omnia alterutram partem ex praedestinatione statuta et definita esse pronunciat, De lib. arbit. lib. 1. sect. 11. Atque dicit sub gratiae vocabulum absconditum esse ab illo fatale decretum, ibidem. Postremo, ipse Augustinus multis in locis cogitur hanc iniquissimam calumniam eluere: Contra 2 Epist. Pelag. lib. 2. cap. 7. et De bono persever. lib. 2. cap. 12. et alibi passim. Haec praemittere volui responsioni nostrae, ut ex quorum lacunis omnia fere adversariorum argumenta hauriantur intelligatis.
